card: Paper card. Question: Can a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy be developed that exhibits superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically avoiding the formation of irradiation-induced dislocation loops under fusion-relevant conditions?. System: Quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature and 3 mtorr pressure; deposition powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) with 20 W bias radio frequency power; film thicknesses of ~100 nm for TEM and ~3 μm for mechanical testing. Test conditions: In situ irradiation with 1-MeV Kr+2 ions at 1073 K (dpa rates 0.0006 and 0.0016 dpa s−1) up to 8 dpa; ex situ irradiation with 3-MeV Cu+ ions at 773 K and 1050 K up to a peak dose of ~17 dpa; thermal annealing up to 1073 K; nanoindentation and nanoDMA testing. Findings: The as-deposited alloy exhibits a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of grains in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and ultrafine regions (100 to 500 nm).; A unique 4-nm lamella-like compositional layering structure was revealed by atom probe tomography (APT) in the as-deposited state.; No irradiation-created dislocation loops were observed even after 8 dpa of irradiation at 1073 K.; Black spots observed after thermal annealing and irradiation were identified as Cr- and V-rich second-phase precipitates (~3 to 5 nm in size) rather than dislocation loops.; The as-deposited samples showed a hardness of 14 GPa with near negligible irradiation hardening.; Modeling predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich precipitates due to negative enthalpies of mixing for W-Ta, W-V, and Cr-V binaries.; Theoretical modeling suggests equal mobilities of vacancies and self-interstitials are the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the exceptional radiation tolerance arises from the equal mobilities of point defects (vacancies and self-interstitials), which maximizes the recombination probability and minimizes defect clustering. This equal mobility is attributed to the rough energy landscape induced by local lattice distortion and chemical disparity in the high-entropy alloy. Additionally, the high density of grain boundaries acts as preferential recombination/annihilation sites for defects.. Limitations: The study was conducted on thin films rather than bulk materials; the exact mechanism for the equal defect mobilities is not fully elucidated beyond the correlation with the energy landscape; the procedure to distinguish precipitates from dislocation loops using TEM breaks down for asymmetric strain fields or non-edge dislocation loops.. Future work: The authors state that the suitability of these alloys for bulk production coupled with their exceptional radiation resistance makes them ideal structural materials for applications requiring extreme irradiation conditions, implying a need for bulk synthesis and further testing.. Quote: "No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed."

card: Paper card. Question: What alloying and scaling conditions lead to the strongest both ductile and stable materials?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) thin films and pillars. Processing: d.c. magnetron co-sputtering on (100) silicon or sapphire substrates at room temperature; Ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) used with 1.2 keV beam energy, 5 mA current, and 35° incidence angle to reduce grain size; Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) used to mill pillars with diameters of ~1 μm, 500, 200, and 100 nm. Test conditions: Microcompression tests at a strain rate of 2 × 10−3 s−1; Thermal annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days in argon atmosphere. Findings: HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ~10 GPa, one order of magnitude higher than the bulk form.; Compressive plastic strains over 30% were achieved in smaller pillars without cracking.; 580-nm Normal HEA pillars show a yield strength of ~5 GPa, while 580-nm IBAD HEA pillars reach ~6.5 GPa.; Smallest IBAD HEA pillars (~70–100 nm diameter) exhibit yield strengths of ~8–10 GPa.; After annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days, HEA pillars retain a high yield strength of ~5 GPa, whereas pure W films show significant grain growth and pore formation.; IBAD HEA pillars exhibit a log–log slope of −0.2 for the relationship between flow stress and pillar diameter, indicating the lowest size dependence among reported pillars.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is attributed to the simultaneous operation of four strengthening mechanisms: lattice friction, Taylor hardening, source-controlled strength, and grain-boundary strengthening. The excellent thermal stability is attributed to relatively low grain-boundary energy due to the highly disordered grain interiors in HEAs, which lowers the driving force for grain-boundary migration compared to pure metals.. Limitations: The text notes that large pillars (>1 μm) experience cracking at strains larger than ~20% and that the smallest pillars (~70–100 nm) show higher scattering levels in strength due to inhomogeneous distribution of grain boundaries.. Future work: The authors state that mechanical tests for small-scale HEAs at high temperatures are still needed to prove their capability as high-temperature materials, and that further work is required to optimize small-scale HEAs for applications, such as determining the best alloying elements and optimized grain and specimen size combinations.. Quote: "Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a reduced-activation WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloy and its W-rich derivatives be fabricated via elemental powder mixing and spark plasma sintering to achieve enhanced hardness and strength for fusion plasma-facing applications?. System: WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloys with W content ranging from 32 to 90 at.% (nominal 30-90 at.%), containing in-situ TiC; specific samples denoted as 32 Ws to 90 Ws.. Processing: Elemental powders (W, Ta, Ti, V, Cr) mixed via Turbula shaker (30 rpm, 3 hours); consolidated via spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1600 °C, 50 MPa axial pressure, 100 °C/min heating rate, 10 minutes dwell time, under vacuum (10⁻³ torr) in graphite molds.. Test conditions: Micro-Vickers hardness test (1 kg load, 10 s dwell); room-temperature compression test (strain rate 10⁻³/s); XRD, SEM-EDS, TEM, EPMA, and ICP-OES characterization.. Findings: Hardness increased to ~790 Hv for the 42 Ws sample, which is more than twofold higher than pure tungsten (~350 Hv).; Compressive yield strength increased to ~2200 MPa for the 32 Ws sample, approximately twice that of pure tungsten.; In-situ TiC formation was confirmed with a volume fraction varying from 1.1% to 8.5% and irregular sizes between 10 to 25 µm.; C15 cubic Laves phases formed in V- and Cr-rich regions in samples with W content exceeding 70 at.% (71 Ws, 77 Ws, 90 Ws).; Relative density increased as W content decreased, with the 32 Ws sample showing the highest density due to liquid-phase assisted sintering.; Grain sizes were ~30–50 µm for samples with 32–63 at.% W (liquid-phase sintering) and ~3 µm for samples with 71–90 at.% W (solid-state sintering).; The BCC crystal structure was confirmed for the HEA matrix with a lattice parameter of 0.317 nm, while TiC exhibited an FCC structure with a lattice parameter of 0.43 nm.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced hardness and strength primarily to solid-solution strengthening caused by differences in atomic radii of the constituents, which hinders dislocation movement, and dispersion strengthening provided by the in-situ TiC particles. Additionally, grain boundary strengthening from TiC and the Hall-Petch effect from smaller grain sizes in high-W alloys contribute to the mechanical properties.. Limitations: The study notes that while the chemical composition meets reduced-activation criteria, the actual reduced-activation behavior, irradiation resistance, hydrogen retention, and high-temperature mechanical properties have not yet been analyzed and require future investigation.. Future work: The authors propose that analysis of reduced-activation behavior, irradiation resistance, hydrogen retention, and high-temperature mechanical properties is necessary prior to utilizing the material as an armor material in future fusion reactors like DEMO.. Quote: "A mechanical examination of the samples revealed a more than twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid-solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening."

card: Paper card. Question: How do AlxCoCrFeNi high entropy alloys behave under ion irradiation, specifically in terms of precipitation?. System: AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.1, 0.75, and 1.5) high entropy alloys. Processing: Arc-melting and drop-casting, with subsequent polishing and preparation for TEM analysis. Test conditions: Irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature, with fluences ranging from 1 × 10^14 to 1 × 10^16 cm^-2. Findings: 1.887e+16; 1.0; 8.1; 7.4; 6.9; 100; 40; 300000000000.0; 100000000000000.0; 1e+16; 43. Mechanism: The high configurational entropy and low atomic mobility of single-phase HEAs reduce the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrain the formation of precipitates, respectively. Limitations: The study only investigates the irradiation responses of HEAs at room temperature, and further studies are needed to understand their behavior at elevated temperatures. Future work: Systematic studies on the irradiation responses of HEAs at elevated temperatures are required for their applications in advanced nuclear systems. Quote: "the high configurational entropy and low atomic mobility"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the Al concentration (3.5 to 54 at.%) influence phase formation and magnetic properties in FeMnCoCrAl high entropy alloy thin films?. System: FeMnCoCrAl high entropy alloy thin films with Al content varying from 3.5 to 54 at.%. Processing: Co-sputtering of equiatomic FeMn, Co, Cr, and Al targets on Si (100) and Al2O3 (0001) substrates; power density varied from 2 to 7.5 W cm−2 for Al target; base pressure 2 × 10−5 Pa; Ar gas at 0.4 Pa; deposition time 22 min; substrate temperature <80 °C. Test conditions: Room temperature magnetic hysteresis (VSM, 5 T max field), temperature-dependent magnetization (10 mT field), XRD (grazing incidence, Co Kα), EDX, Atom Probe Tomography (60 K, 30 pJ laser pulse), TEM (200 kV), electrical resistivity (four-point probe, Van-der-Pauw method). Findings: Al additions to FeMnCoCr (α-Mn structure) induce formation of a body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, with a single BCC random solid solution forming at 8 at.% Al.; The largest saturation magnetization (Ms) of 82 Am2/kg was measured for the film containing 8 at.% Al.; Increasing Al concentration beyond 8 at.% causes a continuous decrease in Ms, dropping to 37 Am2/kg at 20 at.% Al and 7 Am2/kg at 40 at.% Al.; Thin films with Al concentrations of 26 at.% and 40 at.% exhibit nanoscale chemical separation (Al-Co rich regions) not resolved by standard XRD.; The 8 at.% Al single BCC phase thin film possesses a Curie temperature (Tc) greater than 900 K.; The coercivity (Hc) decreases from 13 mT at 4 at.% Al to 2.1 mT at 40 at.% Al, correlating with a reduction in column width from ~54 nm to ~20 nm.; The single phase BCC film containing 8 at.% Al exhibits an electrical resistivity of 151 µΩ cm, which increases with higher Al concentrations.. Mechanism: Al additions stabilize the BCC phase over the FCC phase by forming a pseudogap at the Fermi level. The increase in Ms at low Al content is due to the formation of the ferromagnetic BCC phase, while the subsequent decrease is caused by the dilution of ferromagnetic species (Fe, Co) by paramagnetic Al and lattice distortions from Al's larger atomic radius. Nanoscale segregation in high-Al films further reduces magnetization by reducing ferromagnetic exchange interactions.. Limitations: The thin film synthesis involves high quenching rates, so the composition boundaries for phase formation might deviate from those obtained by near-equilibrium processing. The study notes that more detailed investigations on factors affecting coercivity and magnetic anisotropy are subject of future work.. Future work: More detailed investigations on factors affecting Hc and the effects of magnetic anisotropy are subject of future work. The authors also suggest the material system may enable applications in magneto-caloric devices or high-frequency inductors.. Quote: "Al additions to FeMnCoCr crystallizing in the alpha-Mn structure cause the formation of the body centered cubic (BCC) structure."

W2599853299.title: A TRIP-assisted dual-phase high-entropy alloy: Grain size and phase fraction effects on deformation behavior

card: Paper card. Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: How can strong local compositional disorder in high entropy oxides be exploited to generate tunable magnetic behaviors, ranging from macroscopically ordered states to frustration-driven dynamic spin interactions, and can a simplified model predict the emergence of these states?. System: La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 (L5BO) and Mn-varied variants La(Cr0.15Mn0.4Fe0.15Co0.15Ni0.15)O3 (40% Mn) and La(Cr0.1Mn0.6Fe0.1Co0.1Ni0.1)O3 (60% Mn). Processing: Pulsed laser epitaxy (PLD) on SrTiO3 (STO) and (La0.3Sr0.7)(Al0.65Ta0.35)O3 (LSAT) substrates; films were single-phase, epitaxial, with thicknesses of 56 nm (40% Mn), 58 nm (60% Mn), 62 nm (20% Mn), and ~90 nm for neutron diffraction.. Test conditions: Neutron diffraction on single-crystal films and bulk powder; SQUID magnetometry (field-cooled vs. zero-field-cooled) from low temperatures up to 300 K; Monte Carlo simulations using a classical Heisenberg model.. Findings: L5BO (20% Mn) exhibits robust long-range G-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering with a Néel temperature (T_N) near 180 K in single-crystal films.; Increasing Mn concentration to 40% creates a degenerate tipping point where both AFM and ferromagnetic (FM) phases are percolated, resulting in a horizontal exchange bias shift.; Increasing Mn concentration to 60% shifts the dominant phase to ferromagnetism with a Curie temperature (T_C) of approximately 160 K and no observable exchange bias.; The 20% Mn system shows a vertical loop shift due to uncompensated FM moments within a percolated AFM matrix.; The 40% Mn composition displays an incipient quantum critical point where AFM and FM signals grow simultaneously upon cooling.; A classical Heisenberg model populated with composite parameter states accurately predicted the magnetic phase diagram and critical temperatures.; Exchange bias behaviors, traditionally found in bilayer heterojunctions, were generated in monolithic single-crystal films by manipulating local spin disorder.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high entropy oxide hosts a random distribution of spin (S) and exchange (J) interactions where the dominant magnetic phase is determined by the percolation of specific microstates. Increasing Mn concentration shifts the balance from AFM-dominant (Fe-O-Fe bonds) to FM-dominant (Mn-O-X bonds). At 40% Mn, the system reaches a state where both AFM and FM clusters percolate coherently, creating intrinsic frustration and uncompensated spins at the interface of these coexisting phases, which drives the exchange bias effect without the need for physical heterostructuring.. Limitations: The text notes that computationally intensive first-principles approaches are impractical for high entropy oxides due to the vast number of possible microstates (over 200 nearest neighbor combinations), necessitating the use of a simplified classical Heisenberg model rather than precise quantitative calculations.. Future work: The authors propose that manipulating local spin disorder can be used to design novel Griffiths phases or quantum many-body systems with tunable critical behaviors, and that replacing geometric frustration with exchange frustration on a square lattice may lead to unexpected phase spaces.. Quote: "Single‐crystal La(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 films are used as a model system hosting a magnetic sublattice with a high degree of microstate disorder in the form of site‐to‐site spin and exchange type inhomogeneity."

card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

card: Paper card. Question: Can tensile strain induce a high-temperature ferromagnetic insulator state in undoped, high-symmetry LaCoO3 thin films, and how do oxygen vacancies and Co2+ defects affect this state?. System: LaCoO3 thin films (nearly stoichiometric) grown on (001) SrTiO3 and (001) LSAT substrates; Co2+ defect concentration varied from 0% to ~25%. Processing: Pulsed-laser deposition at 750 °C with laser energy density ~1.5 J/cm2 and frequency 1 Hz; oxygen pressure varied between 1 Pa and 25 Pa; film thickness controlled via in situ RHEED oscillations (5 to 30 unit cells). Test conditions: Temperature range 4 K to 390 K for magnetization and resistivity; X-ray diffraction, STEM-HAADF, Co L-edge/K-edge XAS, XANES, and oxygen K-edge STEM-EELS; DFT calculations with GGA+U (U=5.27 eV, J=1.47 eV) at 3.5% tensile strain. Findings: Tensile-strained LaCoO3 films exhibit a ferromagnetic transition with a Curie temperature (TC) up to 90 K, significantly higher than the ≤16 K of known undoped high-symmetry ferromagnetic insulators.; The ferromagnetic state is strongest in nearly stoichiometric films grown at 25 Pa oxygen pressure, where TC is approximately 85 K.; Reducing oxygen pressure from 25 Pa to 10–15 Pa causes a dramatic decrease in TC and magnetization due to reduced tensile strain and increased nonstoichiometry.; Reducing film thickness below 10 unit cells increases Co2+ defect density, causing TC and magnetization to drop drastically.; Ferromagnetism disappears when the Co2+ defect concentration reaches approximately 10% (1Ov/32Co), with magnetization dropping from 2 μB/Co to 1.6 μB/Co.; At a Co2+ concentration of 12.5% (1Ov/16Co), magnetization decreases dramatically to 0.2 μB/Co due to long-range antiferromagnetic coupling.; At 25% Co2+ concentration, magnetization is close to zero, consistent with a step-function behavior with an inflection point near 10% Co2+.; First-principles calculations confirm that oxygen vacancies introduce extra electrons generating HS Co2+ states that support antiferromagnetic superexchange, suppressing ferromagnetism.. Mechanism: Tensile strain stabilizes a ferromagnetic state in LaCoO3 by promoting high-spin Co3+ ions and enabling ferromagnetic coupling between nearest high-spin and low-spin Co3+ ions. Oxygen vacancies introduce extra electrons that form high-spin Co2+ ions with half-occupied eg orbitals, which support antiferromagnetic superexchange interactions that suppress the ferromagnetic order. The ferromagnetism is robust only when Co2+ concentration is below ~10%; beyond this threshold, long-range antiferromagnetic coupling dominates.. Limitations: The detailed understanding of why the LaCoO3 Curie temperature is surprisingly high relative to other undoped high-symmetry ferromagnetic insulators is not yet clear. The nature of the ferromagnetic insulator state in LaCoO3 films remains partially unresolved regarding the specific roles of strain and oxygen vacancies in different contexts.. Future work: Further exploration is required to achieve a detailed understanding of the high Curie temperature behavior. The results provide a foundation for the growth and design of next-generation quantum-spintronic devices.. Quote: "Here we demonstrate a tensile-strained LaCoO3 film to be a strain-induced high-temperature ferromagnetic insulator."

card: Paper card. Question: How does entropy stabilization in transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) influence reversible lithium storage capacity, cycling stability, and the underlying reaction mechanism compared to medium entropy oxides?. System: Transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) with composition (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O; compared to 4-cation medium entropy oxides (MEO) such as (Co0.25Cu0.25Zn0.25Ni0.25)O and (Co0.25Cu0.25Mg0.25Zn0.25)O. Processing: Nebulized Spray Pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C; 4-cation systems required post-annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h under ambient atmosphere; electrodes cast with 63 wt% active material, 22 wt% Super C65, 15 wt% PVA binder. Test conditions: Galvanostatic cycling in Li-metal coin cells, voltage range 0.01–3 V vs. Li+/Li, specific currents from 50 to 3000 mA g−1, room temperature, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC or EC/EMC electrolyte. Findings: The 5-cation TM-HEO cycled over 300 cycles at 200 mA g−1 with specific capacities stabilizing around 650 mAh g−1 after initial activation.; The 5-cation system achieved a specific capacity of 770 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles following a rate increase to 3 A g−1 for 5 cycles.; Medium entropy oxides (4-cation systems) showed rapid capacity degradation, with the Co-removed variant failing completely after ~10 cycles.; The Coulombic efficiency of the 5-cation TM-HEO stabilized between 99.4% and 99.95% in the range of cycles 60–400.; The 4-cation system without Zn (TM-MEO(-Zn)) exhibited a two-step oxidation process at 1.7 V and 2.2 V, unlike the single-step oxidation of the 5-cation system.; High-loading electrodes (2.3 mg cm−2) maintained Coulombic efficiencies >98.5% and an areal capacity of 1.3 mAh cm−2 after 30 cycles.; No metallic phases or Cu dendrites were detected via TEM/EDX after 100 cycles, despite the conversion reaction mechanism.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the rock-salt structure is preserved as a permanent host matrix during the entire conversion process. While some cations (e.g., Co, Cu) are reduced to metallic states during lithiation, they remain 'trapped' within the defect-rich rock-salt lattice stabilized by unreduced cations (e.g., Mg, Ni). This entropy stabilization lowers the Gibbs free energy, favoring the re-incorporation of reduced cations into the original lattice sites upon delithiation, preventing phase separation and structural collapse.. Limitations: The theoretical capacity cannot be predicted with high accuracy due to unknown additional processes like Zn-Li alloying or intermetallic formation; some 4-cation systems (TM-MEO(-Mg) and TM-MEO(-Ni)) could not be synthesized as single-phase compounds even at high temperatures.. Future work: Further investigations should be pursued to explore the full potential of high entropy oxide electrode materials, including the addition of other cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, V) to develop a modular method for tailoring electrodes to specific needs.. Quote: "The stabilization effect of entropy brings significant benefits for the storage capacity retention of high entropy oxides and greatly improves the cycling stability."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy transition-metal carbides be designed to exhibit tunable plasmonic properties in the near-IR to visible range while maintaining high thermal stability and mechanical hardness?. System: High-entropy transition-metal carbides (PHECs), specifically the archetype HfTa4C5 and a set of 14 six-element alloys (Carbon + 5 transition metals from groups 4, 5, and 6: Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W). Processing: Computational: High-throughput disorder modeling using the Partial Occupation (POCC) method within the AFLOW framework to generate Boltzmann ensembles of superlattices, followed by time-dependent density-functional perturbation theory (TD-DFPT) calculations using VASP and turboEELS. Experimental: Ball-milling of TaC and HfC powders (4:1 ratio) followed by Field Assisted Sintering Technology (FAST) at 2100–2400 °C, 40–55 MPa, and 30–40 min hold times.. Test conditions: Computational: Optical limit (q=0) and varying transferred momentum (q); temperatures up to 1500 K. Experimental: Electron-energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) on HfTa4C5 cross-sections at beam energy 300 keV, with temperatures ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) to 1200 °C.. Findings: HfTa4C5 exhibits a crossover energy (E0) at 2.41 eV (simulated) and 2.7 eV (experimental), marking a metal-to-dielectric transition in the visible range.; The plasmonic response of PHECs can be tuned from the near-IR to visible by varying the transition metal components and their concentration.; Systems 3-HfNbTaTiZrC5 and 14-HfNbTaTiWC5 show the highest effective EELS intensity (h) and lowest energy loss dissipation, indicating good plasmonic properties.; The crossover energy E0 spans a wide range from near-IR to visible, increasing monotonically with the atomic number of constituents within each group.; The screened plasmon resonance in HfTa4C5 remains clearly recognizable up to 1500 K, demonstrating stability far above the melting points of standard plasmonic metals like Ag and Au.; Substitution of Hf with 3d metals (V, Cr) leads to plasmonic resonance deterioration, while group 6 metals (W, Mo) cause broadening of the EELS peak.; The presence of Ta is necessary but not sufficient for obtaining good plasmonic PHECs; the best results come from combining high-Z elements from groups 4 and 5 (Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta).. Mechanism: The plasmonic response arises from a balance between intraband transitions (Drude-like, negative contribution to real dielectric function) and interband transitions (positive contribution). The crossover energy E0 corresponds to the energy where the real part of the dielectric function switches sign, determined by the energy difference (δ) between the Fermi level and the edge of the interband transition band (b2). Higher atomic number elements shift the Fermi level deeper into the d-band, increasing δ and causing a blue-shift in E0.. Limitations: The study does not include time evolution or de-excitation processes of plasmons, which are affected by electron-phonon scattering. Experimental characterization beyond 1500 K is noted as arduous due to equipment limitations. Some systems exhibit high dissipation where peaks cannot be associated with collective plasmon-like oscillations.. Future work: The authors propose using the discovered rules to design tailored high-entropy ceramics with optical properties optimized for specific applications, such as exploiting dissipative systems for photothermal applications or using quasi-neutral elements (Ti, W) to stabilize PHECs while altering mechanical/thermal properties.. Quote: "We chose high-entropy transition-metal carbides because of their exceptional thermal, chemical stability, and mechanical properties."

card: Paper card. Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

card: Paper card. Question: How can an all-dielectric metasurface simultaneously achieve high brightness, large color gamut, narrow reflection bandwidth, and diffraction-limit resolution to meet commercial requirements for structural color?. System: Silicon (Si) nanodisks on a sapphire substrate, combined with a refractive index matching layer (dimethyl sulfoxide, DMSO, n=1.48 or PMMA). Processing: Fabrication on commercially available silicon-on-sapphire (SOS) wafers using electron-beam lithography with PMMA resist, lift-off to create a Cr mask, and reactive ion etching (RIE) in an Oxford Plasma System; optical characterization via bright-field microscopy and spectrometry. Test conditions: Bright-field optical microscopy (×50 objective, NA=0.55 for spectra; ×100 objective, NA=0.9 for resolution), white light illumination, samples tested in air and infiltrated with DMSO (n=1.48) or packaged with PMMA. Findings: The experimentally demonstrated color gamut increased from 78% of sRGB in air to 181.8% of sRGB, 135.6% of Adobe RGB, and 97.2% of Rec.2020 when infiltrated with DMSO.; The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of reflection peaks narrowed to 34–40 nm in DMSO, which is 40% narrower than in air.; Background reflection from the substrate was suppressed to approximately zero when the refractive index matching layer was applied.; High reflectance was preserved at ~74% for magnetic dipole resonance across the visible spectrum with the matching layer.; Spatial resolution reached the diffraction limit with pixel sizes as small as 2 × 2 arrays of nanodisks (center-to-center distances down to 190 nm).; The color impression remained uniform and distinguishable even when pixel sizes were reduced from 5 × 5 to 2 × 2 arrays.; The roughness of the fabricated nanostructures was measured to be smaller than 10 nm with sidewalls nearly 90° in the vertical direction.; Single-crystalline Si provided a gamut area 110% and 238% larger than poly-crystalline and amorphous Si, respectively.. Mechanism: The refractive index matching layer reduces the refractive index contrast between the sapphire substrate and the environment, suppressing background reflection. Additionally, the layer pushes the electric dipole resonance closer to the magnetic dipole resonance, creating destructive interference (Kerker condition) that narrows the reflection bandwidth (FWHM) and enhances color purity.. Limitations: The text notes that previous hybrid nanostructures suffered from incompatible fabrication technologies and deformation of top layers during etching, but states that the current single-crystalline Si approach overcomes these specific limitations; no explicit limitations of the current study are stated beyond the general need for commercialization.. Future work: The authors propose that this research routes a key step towards the commercialization of structural color in dynamic displays, optical security, and information storage.. Quote: "Consequently, the experimentally demonstrated gamut has been increased to around 181.8% of sRGB, 135.6% of Adobe RGB, and 97.2% of Rec.2020."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the role of vibrational contributions in the thermodynamic stability of high-entropy carbides, and under what conditions should they be included in stability predictions?. System: (HfNbTaTiV)C, (HfNbTaTiW)C, and (HfNbTaTiZr)C (referred to as HEC-V, HEC-W, and HEC-Zr). Processing: Computational integration of the Partial Occupation (POCC) algorithm with the AFLOW Automatic Phonon Library (APL); structures relaxed until forces were below 10−3 eV/ℓ; phonon calculations used a displacement magnitude of 0.015 ℓ in supercells with at least 180 atoms; TPOCC set to 2473 K.. Test conditions: Harmonic approximation at temperatures ranging from 0 K to synthesis temperatures; comparison against binary carbide precursors (rock-salt phases) and decomposition products; Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) used for comparison.. Findings: Vibrational contributions shift the transition temperature for HEC-W by approximately 150 K, whereas they have only a small effect on HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; Mass disorder on the cation sublattice destabilizes the high-entropy carbides (increases vibrational free energy), while force constant disorder has a stabilizing effect.; The vibrational entropy change (ΔSvib) for HEC-W is 0.22 kB/atom, which is an order of magnitude larger than the 0.04 kB/atom observed for HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; The Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) incorrectly predicts HEC-V to be more strongly stabilized by vibrations than HEC-W, failing to capture phonon anomalies present in VC.; Vibrational contributions shift the decomposition phase transition temperatures for HEC-V and HEC-W to lower temperatures by 80 K and 160 K, respectively.; The carbide sublattice distorts to accommodate different metal cations, resulting in nearest-neighbor metal-carbon distances that are closer to the average of binary carbides to maximize configurational entropy.; Vibrations alone are insufficient to stabilize HEC-V against decomposition at 2000 K, as the vibrational free energy change is smaller than the distance to the convex hull.. Mechanism: The authors argue that vibrational contributions are significant when precursors or decomposition products have different nearest-neighbor environments or symmetries compared to the high-entropy carbide. Specifically, the lower symmetry of hexagonal WC compared to the rock-salt HEC-W leads to depressed vibrational entropy in the precursor, creating a large stabilization gain upon forming the disordered phase. Conversely, when precursors and the HEC share similar atomic environments (as in HEC-V and HEC-Zr), the vibrational entropy changes are minimal.. Limitations: The study relies on the harmonic approximation, ignoring anharmonic effects which become significant at high temperatures and could stabilize structures with imaginary frequencies; the calculations use the PBE functional which may affect phonon frequencies; the ideal high-temperature configurational entropy is used, which overestimates entropic contributions at lower temperatures; and the study is limited to stoichiometric samples without accounting for vacancies or interstitial carbon.. Future work: The authors suggest that anharmonic contributions should be included to improve accuracy, that the effect of the exchange-correlation functional (e.g., SCAN vs. PBE) on transition temperatures needs investigation, and that defects such as vacancies and interstitial carbon atoms should be explored in future research on high-entropy ceramics.. Quote: "The contribution of vibrations to the stability of high-entropy ceramics is still controversial."

Paper card. Question: How to generate and validate derivative structures for (HfNbTaTi)RC high-entropy carbides to ensure converged vibrational free energy calculations.. Processing: Created 49 ordered representative structures using the AFLOW-POCC algorithm from a rock-salt parent structure (space group: Fm-3m, #225); KPPRA value increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K converged within 1 meV/atom; APL supercells generated using standard conventional representations; relaxation and static calculations performed with exact same k-point densities.. Test conditions: Vibrational free energy convergence target of 1 meV/atom at 300 K; k-point densities required to be identical for relaxation and static calculations to avoid residual force increases.. Findings: 49 ordered representative structures were created for the (HfNbTaTi)RC system.; KPPRA values were increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K was converged within 1 meV/atom.; Using different k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations leads to an increase in residual forces by up to two orders of magnitude.; This residual force increase was observed even at KPPRA values above 20,000.; Standard conventional representations were used to generate APL supercells to achieve a more spherical shape.. Mechanism: The authors argue that maintaining exact same k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations is critical to prevent large residual forces, which can occur even at high KPPRA values if densities differ.. card: Paper card. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at% W, 20 at% Ta, 20 at% Mo, 20 at% Nb, 20 at% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system with 400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere, mixed elemental powders (20-70 µm, irregular shape) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; parameters: laser power 160–244 W, spot size 80 µm, scanning speed 300–700 mm/s, hatch spacing 0.10–0.12 mm, layer thickness 0.3 mm, energy density 38.1–162.7 J/mm³; rotation of 67° per layer. Reference sample produced by Arc Melting Furnace (AMF) with 12 g mixed powder compacted to 50% green density.. Test conditions: Microstructure: SEM, TEM (200 kV), XRD (CuKα, 40 kV/30 mA, 2°/min). Physical: Vickers hardness, compression strength (0.5 mm/min crosshead speed). Electrochemical: Potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl at ambient temperature (0.5 mV/s scan rate, SCE reference).. Findings: Both LPBF and AMF samples formed a single solid phase solution with a BCC crystal structure and a lattice parameter of 3.2 Å.; LPBF samples exhibited a finer average grain size of 10 µm compared to 25 µm for AMF samples.; LPBF samples achieved a maximum density of 95% in advanced trials, compared to 38% in primary trials.; The ultimate compressive strength of the LPBF sample was slightly higher than that of the AMF counterpart.; LPBF samples showed a maximum crack density of 6.4×10⁻⁷ μm⁻².; Sub-grains of approximately 500 nm and high-density dislocations were observed in the LPBF matrix via TEM.; Spherical precipitates of 60–80 nm containing 33 at% V and 7.9 at% W were found at intergranular boundaries in LPBF samples.; Both alloys demonstrated excellent corrosion resistance with an active-passive transition mode in 3.5% NaCl solution.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the distribution of elements to melting temperature differences, noting that vanadium's lower melting point (1910 °C) causes it to solidify at grain boundaries during the final stage, while tungsten's high melting point (3422 °C) and density lead to segregation. The finer grain size and higher strength in LPBF are attributed to rapid solidification characteristics and inherent internal stresses generating dislocations. The presence of precipitates and elemental segregation is linked to the end-stage solidification dynamics and the irregular shape of the mixed elemental powders affecting laser interaction.. Limitations: The authors state that the LPBF process resulted in inherent printing defects such as lack-of-fusion, porosity, and unmelted powder particles, which induced brittleness. They also note that the passivation stability of the LPBF alloy was reduced due to increased surface roughness, leading to current density fluctuations and a higher number of small pits compared to the AMF alloy.. Future work: The authors propose that additional experimental work is required to further optimize printing parameters to obtain improved properties and microstructure characteristics, specifically to reduce printing defects. They also suggest including post-heat treatments to upgrade the homogeneity of the LPBF alloy and its synthesis characteristics.. Quote: "The results disclosed similarities in microstructure, physical properties and electrochemical behavior between HEA WTaMoNbV manufactured by the proposed LPBF process and its counterpart alloy produced by an AMF process."

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?. System: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites. Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.. Test conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.. Findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.; SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.; Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.; HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.; SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.; Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.; Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.; Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.. Mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.. Limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.. Quote: "Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a high-entropy alloy with the composition Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 be successfully produced using Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM) from a blend of elemental powders, and what are the resulting microstructural and compositional characteristics?. System: Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 multi-principle alloy (elemental powder blend of Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Ta). Processing: Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM) using an ARCAM EBM A2 machine; build temperature 920 °C, layer thickness 50 μm, beam speed 80 mm/s, beam current 20 mA (energy density 15 J/mm); two-stage preheat-melt process with semi-sintering; no process parameter optimization was performed.. Test conditions: Post-manufacturing heat treatment in vacuumed quartz ampules for 24 hours at 1000 °C and 1300 °C; microstructure examined via SEM/EPMA (20 kV) and XRD (20–80°); chemical composition analyzed via SEM/EPMA.. Findings: The as-built sample contained 8.4 at % Al instead of the designed 12.0 at % due to evaporation during printing.; The as-manufactured microstructure consisted of two solid solutions: an Al-poor phase (TaMoNb-based, ~1.4 at % Al) and an Al-rich phase (~11.8 at % Al).; Heat treatment at 1000 °C reduced Al content to 8.0 at % and Cr to 24.7 at %.; Heat treatment at 1300 °C further reduced Al to 7.8 at % and Cr to 23.2 at %.; Significant residual porosity was observed in all samples, attributed to non-optimized process parameters.; Heat treatment improved microstructural homogenization but did not reduce residual porosity.; Splatter droplets ('fireworks') contained all five elements, indicating they did not significantly alter the bulk composition of solid samples.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the compositional changes to the evaporation of light metals (Al and Cr) due to high vapor pressure at the electron beam molten pool temperature (up to 2500 °C) and the vacuum environment (10−3 mbar). The formation of two distinct solid solutions (Al-poor and Al-rich) is a result of incomplete homogenization during the rapid melting and solidification of the elemental powder blend, despite in situ alloying occurring.. Limitations: The process parameters were not optimized, leading to notable residual porosity. Heat treatment caused undesirable alloy composition changes (depletion of Al and Cr) due to evaporation in the vacuum ampules.. Future work: The authors conclude that process parameter optimization rather than post-process heat treatment should be performed to reduce the porosity of samples.. Quote: "The main conclusion is that the production of the Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 multi-principle alloy from elemental powder blends using SEBM technique is achievable, but the process parameter optimization rather than post-process heat treatment should be performed to reduce the porosity of samples."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the structural, magnetic, and transport properties of the new equimolar high-entropy alloy FeRhIrPdPt, and how do its dual-phase microstructure and constituent binary alloys explain its magnetic behavior?. System: FeRhIrPdPt (equimolar), FeRh4, FeIr4, FePd4, FePt4. Processing: Arc melting of constituent elements (Fe, Rh, Ir, Pd, Pt) with 99.9% purity in an Ar atmosphere to form 1.5 g button-shaped samples, followed by quenching on a water-chilled Cu hearth and multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity; no heat treatment or deformation applied.. Test conditions: XRD with Cu-Kα radiation; SEM/EDX at room temperature; DC magnetic susceptibility (χdc) between 50–450 K and 2 K; AC magnetic susceptibility (χac) between 3–300 K at frequencies 20 Hz–5 kHz; Electrical resistivity (ρ) between 3–300 K using a dc four-probe method.. Findings: The alloy forms a dual-phase fcc structure with a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase (70 vol.%) and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor phase (30 vol.%).; The main phase is responsible for a canonical spin-glass transition at approximately 90 K.; The minor phase is responsible for a ferromagnetic correlation that appears below 300 K.; FeRh4 and FeIr4 binary alloys exhibit spin-freezing behavior, while FePd4 and FePt4 are ferromagnetic with Curie temperatures of ~400 K and ~317 K, respectively.; The effective magnetic moment (μeff) for FeRhIrPdPt is 3.40 μB/Fe, with a positive Weiss temperature (ΘCW) of 308 K indicating FM correlation.; The Mydosh parameter K for FeRhIrPdPt is 0.007, classifying it as a canonical spin-glass HEA.; Electrical resistivity of FeRhIrPdPt slightly increases on cooling, indicating weak carrier localization, unlike the metallic behavior of the binary alloys.; The dual-phase formation is explained by the pairwise formation enthalpies, where Fe-Pd and Fe-Pt pairings are more robust than Fe-Rh and Fe-Ir.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the dual-phase microstructure results from the thermodynamic preference for specific binary pairings (Fe-Pd, Fe-Pt, Ir-Rh) based on negative formation enthalpies. The magnetic properties arise from the independent contributions of the two phases: the Rh/Ir-rich main phase (analogous to FeRh4/FeIr4) drives the spin-glass transition at 90 K, while the Pd/Pt-rich minor phase (analogous to FePd4/FePt4) drives the ferromagnetic correlation below 300 K. The lack of long-range ordering in the ferromagnetic correlation is attributed to the inhomogeneous magnetic state of the minor phase.. Limitations: The study was limited to as-cast samples without heat treatment or deformation; the thermal stability of the dual-phase microstructure was not investigated.. Future work: The authors state it is important to understand the thermal stability of the alloy to control the microstructure, and to investigate the possibility of multifunctional magnetic properties where the two phases offer different functions.. Quote: "The dual-phase is composed of a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor one."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a combination of machine learning, phenomenological rules, and CALPHAD modeling be used to predict the yield strength of refractory high-entropy alloys in the Al-Cr-Nb-Ti-V-Zr system?. System: Al-Cr-Nb-Ti-V-Zr system. Processing: Vacuum arc melting, with a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, and homogenization annealing at 1200 °C for 10 h. Test conditions: Compression tests at 20 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C, with an initial strain rate of 10−4 s−1. Findings: The surrogate model based on a support-vector machine algorithm showed good accuracy at 20 °C and 600 °C, with a prediction error of less than 20% for all alloys except one.; At 800 °C, the error of prediction was worse than 20% for only two model alloys.; The content of aluminum, chromium, and zirconium have the greatest influence on the specific yield strength.; The effect of vanadium and titanium is lower; an addition of niobium has a negative effect on specific yield strength.; One of the predicted alloys (A5: Al13Cr12Nb20Ti20V35) possesses an excellent combination of strength and ductility in the interval 20–800 °C.. card: Paper card. Question: Which equimolar quinary combinations of 40 metallic elements form thermodynamically stable single-phase solid solutions, and what are the driving factors (mixing enthalpy, melting point, intermetallic competition) governing their formation?. System: Equimolar quinary alloys from 40 elements (e.g., AlCoMnNiV, CoFeMnNiZn, Cantor alloy CoCrFeMnNi). Processing: High-throughput density-functional theory (DFT) calculations using a binary regular solid-solution model; experimental synthesis via arc-melting (AlCoMnNiV) and mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering (CoFeMnNiZn). Test conditions: Thermodynamic stability assessed at temperatures ranging from 800 to 1600 K, with optimal screening at T = 0.9Tm; experimental validation via SEM, XRD, and EDS after heat treatment at 1373 K (AlCoMnNiV) and 1073–1273 K (CoFeMnNiZn). Findings: Identified 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys out of 658,008 candidates (4.6% of combinations).; 74% of the predicted stable HEAs form in body-centered cubic (BCC) structures.; The model achieved a predictive accuracy of 74% at T = 1350 K, outperforming empirical rules and free-energy models.; High melting point (Tm) is the primary driving factor for HEA formation, with nearly 80% of predicted HEAs containing at least one refractory element.; Al and Zn are outliers that form HEAs easily despite low melting points (933 K and 692 K, respectively) due to favorable mixing with high-melting elements.; The mixing enthalpy of solid solutions correlates linearly with the formation enthalpy of competing intermetallics (IMs).; Successfully synthesized and confirmed the existence of BCC AlCoMnNiV (lattice parameter 2.9 Å) and FCC CoFeMnNiZn (lattice parameter 3.635 Å).; The model predicts that substituting Cr with Zn in the Cantor alloy yields the most stable FCC single-phase HEA among Zn-containing variants.. Mechanism: Phase stability is determined by the competition between the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution (driven by configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy) and the free energy of competing intermetallic phases. High melting points allow for high synthesis temperatures where entropic stabilization dominates, while mild mixing enthalpy often correlates with weak intermetallic competition, facilitating solid solution formation.. Limitations: The model does not account for vibrational entropy, magnetic ordering, or short-range ordering, which would increase computational cost; it also struggles to discriminate between HCP and FCC structures due to their small energy difference.. Future work: Future screenings can incorporate vibrational effects, magnetic ordering, and short-range ordering in a tiered approach; the model can be applied to non-equimolar compositions and tailored for specific properties beyond phase stability.. Quote: "We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

Question: How can the compiled mechanical properties of high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be used to assess their potential as structural materials and guide future development?. System: 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), including 3d transition metal, refractory metal (RHEAs and RCCAs), light metal family, and bronzes and brasses HEAs/CCAs families; HEAs defined as alloys with 5 or more principal elements (5-35 at%); CCAs defined as alloys with 3 or more principal components.. Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) at room temperature for 370 alloys; temperature-dependent testing for 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs).. Findings: The database covers mechanical properties for 370 HEAs and CCAs reported between 2004 and 2016.; For 27 refractory HEAs, yield stress and elongation are provided as a function of testing temperature.; The database includes alloy composition, microstructure type, density, hardness, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength, and Young's modulus.; Data entries are organized in a tree-like classification with four families and expanded into classes based on principal element combinations.; The database enables users to browse, search, filter, and plot material property maps using performance indices defined by M. F. Ashby.. Mechanism: The authors explain that HEAs are presumably stabilized by the configurational entropy of mixing, while CCAs encompass a broader range of alloys with single-phase or multi-phase microstructures; the database allows for the evaluation of performance indices for lighter, stronger, and stiffer structures.. Limitations: The properties are not equally populated for every alloy due to the lack of literature data.. Future work: The database can be used to represent various property spaces, calculate performance indices, and enable data mining to extract insights and uncover patterns to guide and accelerate the development of HEAs and CCAs.. card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy materials (HEMs) leverage configurational entropy to overcome the limitations of conventional enthalpy-dominated catalysts, specifically regarding phase stability, active site tunability, and the breaking of scaling relationships in electrocatalysis?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) including PtPdCoNiFeCuAuSn, PtPdRhRuCe, Ru0.44Rh0.30Co0.12Ni0.14, CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10, IrPdPtRhRu, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, and AlNiCoIrM; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) and perovskites; Multimetallic nanoclusters (MMNCs).. Processing: Carbothermal shock (ultrafast joule heating followed by rapid quenching at ~1500 K); Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) reaching 923 K within 5 s; Colloidal synthesis with seed-mediated coreduction and annealing at 600°C; Ionic liquid-assisted cosputtering; Ball milling and solvothermal synthesis.. Test conditions: Ammonia oxidation at 700°C; Ammonia decomposition at 500°C; Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in acidic and alkaline media; Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic and alkaline media; Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic and alkaline solutions; Li-O2 battery cycling.. Findings: Quinary HEA nanoparticles (PtPdRhRuCe) achieved ~100% conversion and >99% selectivity toward NO + NO2 at 700°C with no degradation over 30 hours.; HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst reached a mass-specific rate of 0.74 gNH3 m−2 hour−1 at 500°C, representing improvement factors of ~24 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~19 versus Ru.; Computational models predicted an IrPdPtRhRu HEA composition with a ~40-mV lower overpotential relative to Pt (111) for ORR.; Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni nanoparticles with size less than 2 nm delivered ORR activity comparable to Pt under the same conditions.; Octonary RuIrCeNiWCuCrCo catalyst outperformed quaternary and binary counterparts in long-term operation for Li-O2 batteries due to higher configurational entropy.; GO-supported quinary HEA nanoparticles (FeCoPdIrPt) exhibited enhanced HER activity and stability in alkaline solutions relative to commercial Pt/C catalysts.; HEA catalysts containing five or more elements outperformed binary, ternary, and quaternary alloys in alkaline media due to broad adsorption energy distributions.. Mechanism: Enhanced configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions despite large enthalpic differences, allowing atomic mixing of multiple principal elements. Severe lattice distortion lowers the energy barrier for adsorption and activation, while the diverse local coordination environments and electronic perturbations (ligand effects) create a near-continuum distribution of adsorption energies. This distribution allows the catalyst to access optimal binding strengths for intermediates, breaking the linear scaling relationships that limit conventional catalysts.. Limitations: Low surface area of bulk HEAs limits catalytic utilization; maintaining nanoscale morphology at elevated temperatures is difficult due to migration and aggregation; synthesis of single-phase HEAs requires overcoming thermodynamic barriers; characterization is challenging due to increased compositional and structural complexities; phase segregation can occur if entropy is insufficient to overcome enthalpic differences.. Future work: Further elucidation of structure-property relationships across different HEM subcategories; development of high-throughput synthesis and measurement tools for accelerated materials discovery; deeper mechanistic studies on surface restructuring under reaction conditions; optimization of catalyst stability for noble metal-free applications.. Quote: "The ability to confine multiple principal elements in a single lattice is intriguing for the design of advanced catalysts with desirable activity, selectivity, and stability."

Paper card. Question: How can the configurational entropy in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be leveraged to overcome the miscibility limitations of traditional alloys and enhance catalytic performance for complex reactions like ethanol oxidation?. System: Platinum-group metal (PGM) high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles containing Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, and Pt; specifically compared against physical mixtures of unary PGMs and binary/ternary/quaternary/quinary PGM alloys.. Processing: Prepared using a facile polyol method to synthesize PGM-HEA nanoparticles.. Test conditions: Electrochemical ethanol oxidation reaction in aqueous solution; performance compared against commercial Pd/C, Pd black, Pt/C, and Au@PtIr/C catalysts; cyclic voltammetry used to analyze individual constituent contributions.. Findings: The PGM-HEA nanoparticles exhibited much higher activity relative to commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts.; Negligible activity was observed for the physical mixture of the six unary PGM nanoparticles, confirming the necessity of atomic mixing.; The PGM-HEA delivered a mass activity more than 1.5 times higher than that of the most active catalyst to date (Au@PtIr/C).; The PGM-HEA exhibited the highest current density in the full potential range compared to ternary, quaternary, and quinary PGM alloys.; Pt and Pd are active for ethanol conversion but become poisoned by adsorbed (CO)ad or CHx species.; Os and Ru facilitate the oxidation of (CO)ad, mitigating the poisoning effect for Pt and Pd.; Ir and Ru ensure that dehydrogenation or C─C cleavage occurs at a low potential, while further oxidation hinges on Pt and Pd components.. Mechanism: The atomically mixed metals in HEAs play distinct yet concerted functions: Pt and Pd drive ethanol conversion; Os and Ru mitigate poisoning by oxidizing adsorbed species; Ir and Ru lower the potential for C─C cleavage and dehydrogenation. This synergy allows for efficient and complete oxidation of ethanol involving multiple proton-electron transfers.. Limitations: The text notes that while simple reactions can be triggered by mono- and bimetallic PGMs, it is difficult to drive complex reactions involving multiple proton-electron transfers and intermediate species without the synergistic effects provided by HEAs.. Future work: The authors imply the need to better understand the contribution of each metal to the overall reaction, as demonstrated by their comparison of cyclic voltammetry curves of individual constituents to elucidate specific roles in preventing poisoning and facilitating cleavage.. Quote: "The PGM-HEA nanoparticles efficiently catalyzed the ethanol oxidation reaction, exhibiting a much higher activity relative to that of the commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts, respectively."
