card: Paper card. Question: How does the wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) performance of WNbMoTaZrx (x = 0.5, 1) refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) compare to that of conventional materials?. System: WNbMoTaZrx (x = 0.5, 1) RHEAs, tungsten, cemented carbide, and industrial pure Zr. Processing: Wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) with varying electrical parameters. Test conditions: Orthogonal and single-factor experiments with different processing parameters. Findings: 1. The cutting efficiency (CE) of RHEAs is significantly affected by the pulse-on time (ON), pulse-off time (OFF), and peak current (IP).; 2. The surface roughness (Ra) of RHEAs is mainly dependent on the ON and IP.; 3. The CE of RHEAs can be tuned by optimizing the processing parameters, but it is challenging to tune the surface roughness.; 4. The RHEAs maintain the main BCC1 phase enriched with W and Ta elements after WEDM, while the BCC2 phase enriched with Zr and Nb elements disappears.; 5. The formation of the upper recast layer consisting of re-solidified particles is the main reason for the relatively larger surface roughness of RHEAs.. Mechanism: The WEDM process involves the melting and removal of workpiece materials, and the formation of the upper recast layer consisting of re-solidified particles.. Limitations: The surface roughness of RHEAs is challenging to tune by changing the processing parameters.. Future work: Further understanding of the melting and removal mechanisms of RHEAs during WEDM, and the use of advanced WEDM techniques to improve the surface quality.. Quote: "The CE of RHEAs can be tuned by optimizing the processing parameters, however, it is challenging to tune the surface roughness of RHEAs by tailoring the processing parameters."

Paper card. Question: How do W-containing refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties and neutron irradiation resistance under extreme conditions?. System: W-containing RHEAs, such as VCrFeTaxWx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 1), MoWAlCrTi, TixWTaVCr, and W0.5(TaTiVCr)0.5. Processing: Vacuum arc melting (VAM), mechanical alloying (MA), spark plasma sintering (SPS), and magnetron sputtering (MS). Test conditions: High temperatures (up to 1200 °C), neutron irradiation, and corrosive environments (such as sulfuric acid and NaCl solution). Findings: The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 RHEAs demonstrated improved hardness and exhibited a compressive yield strength exceeding 1000 MPa after annealing at 600 and 800 °C; The MoWAlCrTi RHEA showed excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance, with a specific mass change of only about 0.2 mg/(cm2·h) after exposure to air at 1000 °C for 40 h; The W0.5(TaTiVCr)0.5 RHEA exhibited excellent irradiation resistance, with only slight damage after He+ ion irradiation; The WNbMoTaV RHEA showed superior wear resistance, with a wear rate almost 80% lower than Inconel 718 using an Al ball under a 2000 m sliding distance. Mechanism: The excellent functional properties of W-containing RHEAs are attributed to the formation of dense oxide protective layers, passive films, and solid solution strengthening. Limitations: The number of reported W-containing RHEAs is far less than the theoretically predicted systems, and the effects of different elements on the phase structure, mechanical properties, and functional characteristics of RHEAs are not fully understood. Future work: Further research is necessary to develop new W-containing RHEA systems with high-end properties, to reveal the strengthening and deformation mechanisms of W-containing RHEAs in harsh environments, and to investigate the machining performance of W-containing RHEAs. Quote: "excellent mechanical properties and stability at high temperatures"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the machinability of Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy compare to 304 stainless steel in terms of cutting forces, tool wear, surface quality, and microstructural changes during milling?. System: Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) and X5CrNi18-10 (304) stainless steel. Processing: Face milling using a 12 mm diameter shank cutter with two indexable carbide inserts (grade HSC 05, PVTi coating) on a FIRST MCV 300 vertical milling center; dry cutting conditions; 25 tests using Taguchi method with cutting speed (vc), feed per tooth (fz), and axial depth of cut (ap) varied; radial depth of cut ae = 12 mm (100%); sample dimensions 145 × 15 × 6 mm³ for HEA. Test conditions: Dry cutting; spindle speeds up to 8000 rpm; feed rates up to 103 mm/min; axial depth of cut (ap) ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.42 mm; feed per tooth (fz) ranging from 0.05 mm/tooth to 0.15 mm/tooth; cutting speed (vc) varied across 5 levels; temperature measured via thermo vision camera (0–500 °C range); cutting forces measured with Kistler 9257B dynamometer. Findings: The machinability of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of 304 stainless steel based on the resultant cutting force.; Cutting temperatures ranged from 120 °C to 281 °C, with the maximum temperature (213.2 °C) recorded after about 6 s of processing.; The axial depth of cut (ap) was identified as the main influencing parameter on cutting temperature, with maximum temperatures (240–281 °C) occurring at ap = 0.42 mm.; Maximum flank wear width (VBB max) was 86 µm for the first cutting edge (CE1) and 67 µm for the second cutting edge (CE2).; Maximum crater dimensions on the rack face for CE2 were KBmax = 490 µm and KMmax = 225 µm.; Surface roughness values ranged from 0.39 µm to 2.058 µm, with the best values obtained at minimum feed (fz = 0.05 mm/tooth).; Microhardness of the machined HEA surfaces ranged from 365 HV0.2 to 444 HV0.2, attributed to material inhomogeneity and self-hardening.; XRD analysis showed that patterns for as-cast and machined surfaces were very similar, with no new phases formed during machining.. Mechanism: The superior machinability of the HEA compared to stainless steel is attributed to its specific cutting force behavior, where the resultant force is lower despite higher hardness. The irregular chip fragmentation and surface defects are caused by the inhomogeneity of the cast material and the presence of hard intermetallic phases (e.g., Fe2Al5, FeAl3) which act as micro-edges causing tool wear. Self-hardening effects and oxidation during cutting contribute to the increased microhardness and chip fragmentation, while the similar XRD patterns indicate the material withstands heating cycles without phase transformation.. Limitations: The study was limited to dry cutting conditions and did not evaluate the effects of cooling and lubrication. The research is described as preliminary, and the number of reference XRD patterns available in the database is limited. The study did not cover extended ranges of cutting parameters for finish and rough cuts, nor did it generate predictive mathematical models for material removal rate or tool life.. Future work: More detailed research should be achieved to have a more precise image of the machinability of the HEA by considering the cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting tool life. Furthermore, extended ranges of the cutting parameters should be considered for both finish cut and rough cut and to generate predictive mathematical models to improve processing and optimize cutting parameters.. Quote: "In terms of cutting forces, the behavior of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of stainless steel."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the microstructure and mechanical properties of novel high-strength, low-activation Wx(TaVZr)100−x refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) change with varying W content?. System: Wx(TaVZr)100−x (x = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25) refractory high entropy alloys. Processing: vacuum arc melting under a Ti-gettered, high-purity argon atmosphere, with 12 remelting cycles. Test conditions: room temperature (RT) compression tests at an initial strain rate of 5 × 10−4 s−1. Findings: The RHEAs possess a disordered BCC phase, ordered Laves phase, and Zr-rich HCP phase; The yield strength of the RHEAs increases with increasing W content, reaching a maximum value of 1985 MPa in the W20 RHEA; The hardness value also increases with increasing W content; The microstructure of the RHEAs changes significantly with increasing W content, from a slender dendrite shape to a coarser dendrite shape; The distribution of dendrites becomes denser with increasing W content; Microcracks initially form in interdendritic regions during compression, and molten droplets also form in interdendritic regions on the fracture surface; The fracture mode of the RHEAs changes from initial intergranular fractures to a mixed fracture mode featuring the coexistence of both intergranular and transgranular fractures with increasing applied load. Mechanism: The improvement in strength and hardness is mainly due to solid solution strengthening and the increase in dendritic regions. Quote: "The RHEAs demonstrate high strength and hardness, with these properties being higher than in most reported tungsten-containing RHEAs"

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy REBCO nanocomposite films be successfully synthesized using chemical solution deposition (CSD) and what are their superconducting properties?. System: Gd0.2Dy0.2Y0.2Ho0.2Er0.2Ba2Cu3O7−δ with 12 mol% BaHfO3 nanoparticles. Processing: Chemical solution deposition (CSD) using the TFA-MOD route with optimized growth parameters: Tg = 810 °C and pO2 = 100 ppm. Test conditions: Temperature range: 30 K to 77 K, magnetic field range: 0 T to 14 T. Findings: High-quality Gd0.2Dy0.2Y0.2Ho0.2Er0.2Ba2Cu3O7−δ nanocomposite films with 12 mol% BaHfO3 nanoparticles were successfully synthesized; Tc = 91.9 K and Jsfc = 3.5 MA cm−2 at 77 K; Jc values at 30 K are larger than those of single-RE samples; HEO films show promising performance at high fields and low temperatures; RE distribution is homogeneous in the matrix without forming clusters. Mechanism: The homogeneous distribution of RE3+ ions in the matrix creates point-like pinning centers, which explain the superior performances of these samples at low temperatures. Limitations: The Jc values of HEO films are still lower than those of medium-entropy REBCO films, indicating a need for optimization of the composition. Future work: Further studies are needed to optimize the composition of HEO films and to investigate the effect of average RE ion size and its variance on the final properties of the films. Quote: "the first CSD-grown high-entropy (HE) REBCO nanocomposite films were successfully synthesized"

card: Paper card. Question: How do point defect clusters in high-temperature superconductors lead to the formation of ferromagnetic clusters embedded within the superconductor?. System: YBa2Cu3O7-δ (Y123) thin films with Y124 intergrowths. Processing: Chemical Solution Deposition (CSD) with pyrolysis and crystallization steps. Test conditions: Temperature range: 1.6-100 K, magnetic field range: -6 to 6 T. Findings: Cu di-vacancies decorated by three O vacancies (2V Cu+3V O) are the most stable type of Cu defect; The four Cu atoms neighboring the defect carry a total moment of 1.3 μB per defect; The magnetic moments of the Cu atoms in the double chain and in the CuO2 planes in the vicinity of the defects are of the same sign, i.e., ferromagnetically coupled; The system behaves like a superparamagnet, with a Curie dependence of the effective spin moment with temperature; The field dependence of the total magnetization can be well fitted by the Langevin function, indicating superparamagnetic behavior of isolated ferromagnetic clusters. Mechanism: The ferromagnetic order of the Cu atoms in the superconducting Y123 films is explained in terms of a superparamagnetic behavior of isolated ferromagnetic clusters, even below the superconducting transition temperature. Limitations: The restriction on the size of the supercells that can be used in DFT calculations limits the ability to comment on long-range magnetic ordering. Future work: Investigating the role of the novel ferromagnetic behavior in pinning vortices, and searching for the presence of magnetism in the vicinity of superconductivity in other defective perovskite-based systems. Quote: "the ferromagnetic order of those Cu belonging to the CuO2 planes and surrounding the O-decorated Cu vacancies does not vanish when superconductivity sets in at T c"

card: Paper card. Question: Can a simple YBCO superconductor formulation with Y2O3 nanoparticles be used to produce high-performance 2G HTS wires for fusion applications?. System: YBa2Cu3O7 (YBCO) with Y2O3 nanoparticles. Processing: Pulsed laser deposition (PLD) on a Hastelloy C276 substrate with a buffer layer architecture based on MgO textured using ion beam assisted deposition. Test conditions: Measurements at 4.2 K and 20 K in magnetic fields up to 20 T and 31.2 T. Findings: Record engineering current density of over 1000 A/mm2 at 20 K, 20 T; Record engineering current density of over 2000 A/mm2 at 4.2 K, 20 T; High critical current values in the 220-270 A/4 mm range at 20 K, 20 T; High critical current values in the 450-570 A/4 mm range at 4.2 K, 20 T; Low statistical scatter in the ratio of the Ic at 4.2 and 20 K to that at 77 K in self-field; YBCO wire outperforms GdBCO wire by a factor of 1.5 to over 2.5 in the entire range of magnetic fields studied at temperatures of 65 K and below. Mechanism: The Y2O3 nanoparticles provide isotropic pinning amplified by point defects arising from the epitaxial strain induced by the presence of the nanoparticles, and the high CuO2 plane hole doping level minimises the electronic anisotropy and strengthens the vortex pinning of YBCO. Future work: Investigation of the effects of the size, concentration and orientation type of the nanoparticles on the pinning properties of YBCO. card: Paper card. Question: What are the synthetic strategies toward high entropy materials and how can they be used to achieve maximum disorder?. System: High entropy materials, including alloys, oxides, chalcogenides, and other multicomponent systems. Processing: Atom-up synthetic approaches, including solvothermal synthesis, carbothermal shock synthesis, sol–gel synthesis, and molecular-precursor approaches. Findings: High entropy materials can be synthesized using atom-up approaches, which allow for homogeneous mixing of elements at the atomic scale; Atom-up approaches can be used to synthesize a wide range of high entropy materials, including alloys, oxides, and chalcogenides; The molecular precursor approach is a versatile and scalable technique for synthesizing high entropy materials; High entropy materials can exhibit unique properties, such as entropy stabilization, sluggish diffusion, and the cocktail effect; The number of unique sites in a high entropy material can be extremely large, making it challenging to model and characterize these materials. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy of high entropy materials can be achieved through the use of atom-up synthetic approaches, which allow for homogeneous mixing of elements at the atomic scale. Limitations: The authors note that the synthesis of high entropy materials can be challenging, particularly when it comes to achieving homogeneous mixing of elements at the atomic scale. Future work: The authors propose the development of suitable modeling approaches as an important complementary research direction to synthesis and characterization protocols, and suggest the use of artificial intelligence for scaling atomistic simulations to more realistic supercells. Quote: "High-entropy materials are a nascent class of materials that exploit a high configurational entropy to stabilize multiple elements in a single crystal lattice"

card: Paper card. Question: Can alloying be used to optimize the physical properties of tin sulfide/selenide solid solutions for energy applications?. System: Tin sulfide/selenide solid solutions, specifically Pnma and rocksalt Sn(S1–xSex), Sn(S1–xSex)2, and Sn2(S1–xSex)3. Processing: High-throughput first-principles computational modeling and statistical thermodynamics, with supercell expansions and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Findings: The formation of Pnma Sn(S1–xSex) and Sn(S1–xSex)2 solid solutions is predicted to be facile; Rocksalt Sn(S1–xSex) solid solutions are predicted to be metastable, but may be accessible under certain synthesis conditions; Sn2(S1–xSex)3 solid solutions with low Se content are predicted to be accessible; The bandgap of the solid solutions can be tuned by varying the composition; The lattice thermal conductivity is predicted to decrease with increasing Se content. Mechanism: The alloying of tin sulfide and selenide phases leads to a predictable variation of the bandgap, density of states, and optical properties with composition, allowing for the optimization of material properties for energy applications. Limitations: The calculations do not include vibrational contributions to the free energy, and the lattice thermal conductivity is not directly calculated. Future work: The exploration of methods for analyzing more quantitatively the effect of alloying on the lattice dynamics, such as using energetics calculations to parameterize an empirical force field. Quote: "alloying affords facile and precise control over the electronic, optical, and vibrational properties"

Paper card. Question: How do the thermodynamic, electronic, and vibrational properties of Snn(S1–xSex)m solid solutions change with composition, and what are the implications for energy applications?. System: Snn(S1–xSex)m solid solutions, including Pnma Sn(S1–xSex) and Sn(S1–xSex)2. Findings: The bandgap of Sn(S1–xSex)2 can be tuned down to the theoretical optimum for photovoltaic applications; Increasing Se content in Pnma Sn(S1–xSex) decreases the bandgap, but does not significantly improve optical absorption; Alloying can allow the band levels to be adjusted for a better electrical match to other device components; The entropic stabilization obtained by alloying may reduce or prevent undesirable chemical reactions at interfaces; Pnma Sn(S1–xSex) solid solutions with high Se content can improve thermoelectric properties over the champion SnSe material. Mechanism: The authors propose that the systematic composition dependence of the bandgap, band-edge positions, and dielectric properties in the solid solutions can be used to fine-tune optoelectronic properties for energy applications. Limitations: The predicted metastability of the majority of the Sn2(S1–xSex)3 and all of the rocksalt Sn(S1–xSex) compositions implies that preparing and working with these materials in bulk would be challenging. Future work: Future developments toward quantitative modeling of the composition dependence of the lattice dynamics and thermal transport will make this a valuable addition to the growing capabilities of computational materials design. Quote: "providing a means to fine-tune the optoelectronic properties for their proven photovoltaic and photocatalysis applications"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the structural tunability of high-entropy materials (HEMs), specifically the antisite disordering and lattice distortion, be leveraged to optimize catalytic performance and energy storage capabilities compared to traditional alloys or compounds?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) such as PtPdRhRuCe, CoMoFeNiCu, AlNiCoFeX; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) such as (MgCoNiCuZn)Ox, (CoCuMgNiZn)Ox, Li-containing entropy-stabilized oxyfluorides; High-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs); High-entropy borides (HEBs), carbides (HECs), sulfides (HESs), and nitrides (HENs). Processing: Synthesis methods include carbothermal shock (CTS) with thermal shock at ~2,000 K within 55 ms; fast-moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) heating to ~923 K within 5 s; ultrasonication-assisted wet-chemistry with local temperatures up to ~5,000°C; electrodeposition confining precursors to water nanodroplets within 100 ms; solid-state sintering; solvothermal synthesis; and mechanochemical methods. Test conditions: Catalysis tested at temperatures up to 1500 K and reaction temperatures of 305 °C or 155 °C for CO oxidation; electrocatalysis performed at ~80 °C in acidic and basic electrolytes; battery cycling at rates up to 2000 mA/g; supercapacitor testing in 1 m KOH solution at 100 mV/s scan rate. Findings: PtPdRhRuCe NPs achieved ~100% conversion and >99% nitrogen oxide selectivity for ammonia oxidation with no activity degradation.; Quinary CoMoFeNiCu NPs on carbon nanofiber showed a more than 20 times improvement in NH3 conversion rate versus Ru catalysts.; Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Zn0.2O HEO achieved 98% conversion of benzyl alcohol in only 2 h under solvent-free aerobic oxidation.; Ni20Fe20Mo10Co35Cr15 HEA catalyst exhibited an overpotential of 107 mV in acidic solutions, comparable to Pt sheet.; Nanoporous AlCuNiPtMn exhibited a half-wave potential of 0.945 V in acidic media, representing a ~16-fold mass activity of Pt/C for ORR.; AuAgPtPdCu HEA catalyst achieved a faradaic efficiency of about 100% toward gaseous products at -0.3 V for CO2 reduction.; Rock-salt (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O anode delivered an initial capacity of 446 mAh/g and 256 mAh/g after 100 cycles in a full cell.; Nanoporous AlCoCrFeNi HEA exhibited a high volumetric capacitance of 700 F/cm3 and excellent cycling stability of over 3,000 cycles.. Mechanism: The authors attribute enhanced performance to the 'high-entropy effect', 'lattice distortion effect', 'sluggish diffusion effect', and 'cocktail effect', which stabilize single-phase solid solutions and create diverse local electronic structures and adsorption energies. The large number of atomic sites allows tuning of surface electronic structures and adsorption energies, while the uniform configuration leads to severe lattice distortion that increases the activation barrier of diffusion, improving kinetic stability.. Limitations: The fundamental correlations between compositions and phases (e.g., phase diagrams) are not clear; the surface structures of HEMs may not be preserved at working conditions; productivity of HEA NPs via CTS is very low; the actual contribution of entropy versus enthalpy to Gibbs free energy is difficult to determine; and the surface structure of HEMs is more complicated than current catalysts.. Future work: Future work includes enhancing productivity for industrial applications, developing theoretical investigations using DFT and machine learning to design proper HEMs, achieving precise structural control of size, shape, and composition, developing 3D characterization techniques like electron tomography and APT, and exploring new types of HEMs with more than five elements.. Quote: "Precursor of metal salt mixtures was thermally shocked at ~ 2,000 K within 55 ms (as shown in Figure 2A), alloying up to eight dissimilar elements into single-phase solid-solution NPs"

card: Paper card. Question: Can high entropy oxides (HEOs) be used as efficient catalysts for electrochemical water oxidation?. System: Hexanary high-entropy oxides (HEOs) with compositions such as [Al0.35(Mg, Fe, Cu, Ni, Co)0.65]3O4. Processing: Sol-gel synthesis method using citric acid as the chelating agent and ammonia solution to maintain pH at 7. Test conditions: Cyclic voltammetry in 1M KOH with 1M methanol as the facilitator. Findings: Non-equiatomic HEOs exhibited higher catalytic output current than equiatomic HEOs; Compositions with higher Cu and Al contents exhibited greater efficiencies toward catalysis; The maximum OER current density was 94.3 mA cm−2 using NEHEO with 2M methanol; HEOs can be used for further EC processes, including methanol oxidation; The catalytic platforms were stable over the experimental time scale. Mechanism: The high entropy of mixing or stabilization, termed configurational entropy, is responsible for the formation of a single phase of as-synthesized hexanary HEOs. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of HEOs as catalysts for electrochemical water oxidation.
